title: Gutenberg's movable-type printing press at Mainz
summary: In the 1450s Johannes Gutenberg and his partners in Mainz turned out printed books from cast metal type in quantity, culminating in the 42-line Latin Bible of about 1454–1455; within fifty years presses operated in some 205 European cities.
card: Gutenberg's Mainz workshop was making schoolbooks and indulgence forms in cast type by 1454, and a 643-leaf Latin Bible in two columns of 42 lines followed by 1455, in an edition of roughly 150 copies. A lawsuit by his financier Johann Fust in November 1455 ended their partnership, and Fust and Peter Schoeffer then ran their own press. The craft left Mainz with journeymen, and by 1500 books were being printed in about 205 European cities for a fraction of their former price.
what:
Johannes Gutenberg (c. 1400–1468) developed in Mainz, on the Rhine, a way of printing whole books from individually cast metal letters set into pages and inked and pressed onto paper or vellum. A fifteenth-century recollection by the Cologne printer Ulrich Zel put the start in 1450, and economic historians date the first press to between 1448 and 1450. Nobody knows when Gutenberg's first usable type, a large square Gothic face known from its schoolbook and calendar fragments as the DK type, was ready. Princeton University Library's curators think Donatus grammars set in it, and a German prophetic text, were probably on sale by 1453.

The earliest firm date for European printing is 22 October 1454, on a fragment of a 31-line indulgence form issued at Erfurt. Gutenberg had contracted to print such forms in the late summer of 1454 for the Cyprus indulgence campaign, which was raising money against the Ottoman advance. In the same years his shop set the 42-line Bible: 643 large folio leaves intended to bind in two volumes, begun in 40-line columns and then changed to 42, with four compositors working on four sections at once. After eleven quires the print run was raised, and at least 120 paper and perhaps 40 vellum copies were produced, a figure that fits contemporary reports of 158 or 180 copies in 1455. Initials and headings were added by hand in colour.

Gutenberg's financier Johann Fust sued him in late 1455 over the costs of the joint 'work of the books'; the notarial record of that dispute is dated 6 November 1455. Fust then partnered with the scribe Peter Schoeffer, and their Psalter of 14 August 1457 was the first printed book to name its makers and give the date. After Mainz was captured in October 1462, workers dispersed. From 1470 to 1500 printing reached some 240 further towns, and it was the printing of books in cast type, not its first invention anywhere, that this record covers: movable type had been used earlier in Korea and China.

uncertainty.note: Start: Dittmar (2009) dates the first press to 1448–1450 and Ulrich Zel's recollection in the 1499 Cologne Chronicle says 1450; Princeton's curators think the first schoolbooks in the DK type may date to 1453 or a little earlier but call this probable, not provable. The earliest firm date is 22 October 1454 (Erfurt indulgence). End: the 42-line Bible is dated about 1454–1455 and 'probably completed late in 1455' (Library of Congress); the Harry Ransom Center gives 1454–1456.

how: Gutenberg's workshop made the first usable European printing type in the early 1450s, the large square Gothic DK type, and improved it into a finer text face. Type was cast in metal, set letter by letter into lines, locked into pages and printed on a press, so a page could be re-used or distributed in standing type for months. The Bible shop printed schoolbooks on vellum first, then the Cyprus indulgence forms in autumn 1454, and set the Bible by four compositors working on four sections at once. After eleven quires the edition size was raised and those quires reprinted. Fust provided loans for paper, vellum, ink and an apparatus; the dispute over those sums reached court in 1455. Printed sheets were sold across long distances, and Mainz workers later taught others, especially after the city's capture in 1462.
why_it_matters: A scribe, one early printer boasted, could produce in a year what a press produced in a day, and the cost fell accordingly: Dittmar finds that book prices fell by at least 65 percent between 1450 and 1500. Printing was in 205 cities by 1500. Its first economic effect is measurable: cities that gained a press in the 1400s grew about 60 percent faster in the following century than comparable cities without one. Its religious effect is also measurable: in the Holy Roman Empire, cities near a press by 1500 were far more likely to be Protestant by 1600 (Rubin). The press also changed what survived: Princeton's curators note that texts which did not reach print tended to fall rapidly out of use, while almost all school and university texts were printed. Historians disagree about how far printing itself, rather than social and political forces, drove these changes: Eisenstein stressed standardisation, while Johns showed early printed books were often unreliable and pirated. Had Gutenberg's shop failed, movable type would probably still have spread, since concurrent attempts are reported at Avignon and Haarlem and the Chinese and Korean traditions already existed; but the Mainz-centred pattern of diffusion, with journeymen leaving the Rhine for Rome, Cologne, Venice and Paris, would not have been the same.

related.title: Protestant Reformation
related.because: Rubin's analysis finds that cities with a press by 1500 were far more likely to turn Protestant by 1600, consistent with cheap print carrying reform ideas to many readers, though how far print drove the Reformation remains debated.

perspectives.holder: Elizabeth Eisenstein (The Printing Press as an Agent of Change, 1979), as summarised by Blair Worden
perspectives.account: Printing standardised and systematised knowledge by giving readers a shared reference text in place of corrupted manuscript copies, and so acted as an agent of change in the Reformation and science.

perspectives.holder: Adrian Johns (The Nature of the Book), as summarised by Blair Worden
perspectives.account: Early printed books lacked built-in authority, since piracy and plagiarism were common; fixity had to be built by printers, authors and institutions, so print was a vehicle shaped by social forces rather than an independent cause. Worden suggests Johns overstates the case.

perspectives.holder: Princeton University Library curators on printing's origins and spread
perspectives.account: The date of Gutenberg's first usable type is unknown; the earliest firm date is October 1454. The Mainz war of 1461–1463 is widely believed to have driven the spread, plausibly for Rome and Cologne, but Bamberg and Strasbourg printing predates it and some Dutch printing cannot be tied to Mainz.

Gutenberg was developing the technology in Strasbourg before Mainz, and concurrent attempts are reported at Avignon and Haarlem, but the breakthrough was at Mainz and the technology diffused from there.
